utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Major Bower.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My name is Stephen Sayers. Together with my colleague, Mitko Naumovski, we represent the accused Dario Kordic. Over to my left is Mr. Kovacic and his colleague Mr. Mikulicic, and they represent the co-accused Mario Cerkez. Major, you have been a career officer in the British army for the last 16 or so years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you reviewed any milinfosums that were prepared by the 1st Battalion of the Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire in preparation of your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say, Major, that you arrived in Central Bosnia in April of 1993 and were confronted with a confusing, complex, civil war with multiple parties representing the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In the starkest outline, would it be fair to say that the Croats and the Muslims were basically surrounded by Serbian forces, Bosnian Serb army forces, to the west, to the north, and essentially to the south, with a few isolated pockets, but generally speaking that's pretty accurate; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very, very broad outlines, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Within the area into which the Muslim forces and the HVO forces had been compressed, there were also isolated pockets of Croats that were fully surrounded by ABiH forces; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then within those isolated pockets, there were even smaller pockets that were surrounded by HVO forces such as, for example, Stari Vitez, Novi Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Within those towns, basically there were clearly-divided front lines that separated HVO forces on the one side and Muslim forces on the other; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Okay. Would it also be fair to say, sir, that throughout the six-month duration of your tour as a G-5 liaison officer for the Prince of Wales Own Regiment, all males in the country between the ages of 16 and 60 were mobilised to fight?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly what ages, but certainly it appeared able-bodied males were certainly engaged in military duties at some time or another. As to exact ages, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree that it was absolutely routine, in the Croat enclaves where the Muslim forces and the HVO forces were warring, it was absolutely routine for the two combatants to blame each other for incidents that arose during the course of your tour?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a certain amount of denial of responsibility, I would sense it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On both sides?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And also mutual finger pointing at the other side to try to allocate blame; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very rarely would people agree to accept responsibility for actions that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it, sir, you were interviewed first by investigators representing the Prosecution on August the 13th of 1996. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be in the summer of '96. I can't remember the exact date, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Subsequently, approximately eight months later, April the 9th and 10th, 1997, you gave a statement to the investigators for the Prosecution which you subsequently reviewed and signed?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you reviewed that statement in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You were asked, I gather, to record every incident of significance in your tour, to the extent that you could recollect; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken through the six-month tour and asked to note what I could remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As you prepared your statement, you had access to milinfosums, which you reviewed, and also a contemporaneous diary that you kept; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was interviewed in April '97, I didn't have access to the military information summaries, but I had access to a notebook which I had maintained during the tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You would agree, wouldn't you, that Mr. Kordic's name is not mentioned anywhere in your April 1997 statement?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I'm aware, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have previously given testimony, I believe, in the Blaskic case on June the 5th and June the 29th of 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you review a transcript of the testimony that you gave in that case as you prepared for your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree that in the 150 or so pages of testimony that you gave during those two days, the name Dario Kordic is never mentioned by you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it was, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a minor point of detail and precision. My understanding is that you arrived in Split, Croatia, on April the 24th, 1993, to take up your duties.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And travelled to Vitez the very next day?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You left Central Bosnia on November the 7th, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Major, that you do not yourself actually speak any Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just address one general subject, your duties as a G 5 liaison officer. I believe that you said that you are responsible for humanitarian aid and affairs in the BritBat area of responsibility as a G 5 liaison officer; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe also that then Captain Lee Whitworth was the liaison officer specifically delegated to cover the Vitez area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. He was the military liaison officer for that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Captain Boris Cowan was the liaison officer for Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, your area of responsibility covered Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik, and Zenica, but did not include places such as Kakanj, Zepce, or Vares; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a regular basis I would not go to those areas, but occasionally I would if requested to by the aid agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe it's true to say that you visited Busovaca only very occasionally during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During the course of your tour, sir, you used your armoured fighting vehicles regularly to evacuate injured Muslims from Stari Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was actually equipped with soft-skin vehicles. I would only use armoured vehicles if the area I was going into was -- there was still active fighting going on and there was danger to me. Rarely I would use armour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In one of the operations you actually smuggled an injured man out of Stari Vitez along with Dr. Enisa Mulalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then, at her request, you smuggled her back into Stari Vitez after depositing the injured person at hospital facilities in the city of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, after he had been stabilised but then announced dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you started out your duties, Major, isn't it true that you attempted to keep count of the actual casualties that you encountered in your area of responsibility, but this soon fell by the wayside because the numbers were simply too large to count accurately, on all sides?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never consciously kept score. I merely kept a log more of the names in case I had to trace them later for the benefit of family members. That was generally the reason I kept notes, but keeping score was not an aim that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, I'm just referring to the testimony that you gave in the Blaskic case, where you stated on page 9451 that "When we first arrived, we thought we would keep a count, but the count was too great, so we didn't bother." And that's what I was getting at, and that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the whole of the Brit Battalion area, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, the situation you encountered when you arrived in Central Bosnia, and actually throughout the time that you spent there, involved front lines pretty much along the main supply routes; isn't that true to say?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of front lines which I crossed happened to be on the main supply routes, the main roads. That was where we travelled mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the objective of the Muslim forces, at least one of their objectives, was to secure the mountain road linking Zenica to Travnik and actually passing through the village of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether it was one of their objectives or not, but it was certainly what they achieved later on in the tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In the statement on page 6, the 1997 statement -- and I don't think this is different from what you said-- it says, "The ABiH were attempting to secure the mountain road linking Zenica to Travnik which passes by Guca Gora." That's fair to say, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's certainly a period of action which happened during the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To the north of this area, that was the area of operations, as far as you were aware, of the 7th Muslim Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were reports, certainly, that they had been in this area and had been involved in fighting at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Throughout the time of your tour, the six months that you spent in Central Bosnia, there was pressure from the ABiH forces on the Croat forces, generally from the north, compressing the forces southward into the Vitez\Busovaca pocket; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly ebb and flow of pressure from ABiH forces towards HVO forces, along sort of an east/west line, from the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During your tour, Muslim forces actually launched several attacks aimed at capturing points on the main supply route east of Vitez; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly at that time. It happened on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would concede, as a military man with a lot of experience in a fine army, that control and protection of main supply routes is a valid and indeed important military objective, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one question on the political structure of the civilian government in Vitez: Did you have occasion to interact very frequently with the civilian governmental authorities in Vitez, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On arrival in Central Bosnia, generally we started with the mayor of Vitez, but as the situation became more complex, it rapidly deteriorated that we needed to speak to a higher authority and tended to speak directly with the military elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. But you, yourself, weren't involved in those high-level negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the high level. That was left to the commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you had a few meetings with the president of the HVO civilian government in Vitez, Ivica Santic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Mr. Anto Valenta?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your opinion, Mr. Santic did not appear to have any authority to facilitate your access through crowds of civilians or military forces outside of Kruscica, did he, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave some testimony about conclusions relating to the authority of Colonel Blaskic. Just to be absolutely clear, you never actually met him yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw him when he came to meetings but never actually interacted on a professional basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So throughout the six months you spent in the area, you never actually spoke to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you did understand that he was responsible for all of the HVO forces in the Lasva Valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I was aware of the chain of command and where he was in, and that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That included all the HVO forces in your area of responsibility, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You testified in your direct examination yesterday, Major, that on arrival in Vitez, you received a briefing from the military intelligence officer regarding the chain of command in the HVO. That, I take it, was captain Simon Harrison?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were briefed that all of the various groups within the HVO in the Lasva Valley were under the direct command of the 3rd Operations Zone commander, Colonel Blaskic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That included the HOS units about which you testified yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the very, very first briefing, it was generally outlined, and obviously, as we got more information, it was obviously constantly updated. I can't say exactly whether it was the very first one or subsequently over the next couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. But the point I'm making is that all of the units about which you've given testimony -- the HOS, the Vitezovi, the military police and its subunits -- those fell directly under the command of the commander of the Operative Zone, Colonel Blaskic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was explained to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed the briefing that you received, and which was constantly updated regarding the chain of command, enabled you to make the best use of your time in dealing with issues such as access to front lines by knowing exactly to whom you should go in order to arrange that free passage; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It would be accurate, factually accurate, to state that whenever you wanted to achieve something or to acquire permission to do something, you invariably went to the military chain of command rather than to the civilian chain of command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level I was operating in, yes, that was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to one different subject, the chain of command in the opposing forces on the Muslim side. Were you briefed as to the identity of the commander of the Muslim forces in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the co-headquarters, I was briefed and met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that gentleman, I take it, was General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that as commander of the 3rd Corps in Zenica, he had approximately 10 to 12.000 troops under his command?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In approximate figures, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, sir, that around the time of one of the incidents which we talked about, and we'll cover that in slightly more detail in a few minutes, but around June the 10th of 1993, BritBat was informed by General Hadzihasanovic that it would have to have his permission in order to obtain access to any territory controlled by the 325th Mountain Brigade between the towns of -- or the town of Vitez and the city of Zenica, correct, and that was on June the 10th, 1993, around the time of the Convoy of Joy incident?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if it was the passage which was termed the mountain road going through Poculica, yes, there was -- at the Zenica side of the road, there was a checkpoint which we requested to have permission to transit through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you ever briefed about the objectives of the 10 or 12 thousand troops under the command of General Mehemed Alagic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just show you a milinfosum from your battalion, sir, number 72, dated July the 10th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D121/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I only have one question about this, Major. It appears on page 3 under paragraph number 10. Do you ever recall, in your commanding officer briefings, being told that General Alagic was in command of about 12.000 BiH troops and that his current mission was to capture the remaining Croat enclave at Vitez and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I vaguely remember it. But as to detail and when, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fair enough, and that's understandable after the passage of a substantial period of time. In addition, there's reference to the immediate tactical objective of the ABiH forces fighting in July of 1993, and that was to capture the ammunition factory. Were you aware of that tactical objective?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was certainly something which appeared on a frequent basis as a general objective of what they would like to have captured within the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave some testimony regarding the visit that you made to the village of Ahmici just at the beginning of your tour. You actually visited refugees from Ahmici in housing facilities in Zenica; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did visit the population that had been taken to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Major, that in your opinion, anyway, their housing conditions were appalling conditions?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to another subject, if I may, the testimony that you gave concerning your encounter with some HVO troops approximately the end of May 1993. That encounter occurred in the vicinity of the village of Krnjace [phoen], isn't that correct, the item that you circled as Item 1 in Exhibit Z2624?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in that area I marked that map. After some considerable time, that's the general area I believe I was in at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that that area is about five kilometres north of Mount Tisovac?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name, no, I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, can you recall the exact date of this encounter or is it just a vague memory?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's a vague memory in that it was very early on in the tour, and it was some time in May is my -- my journal notes started very shortly after this and as a result of this, so it was before the time that I started making notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So it would be fair to conclude, obviously, that there's no reference in your contemporaneous journal to that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any reference to that incident in a milinfosum prepared by the information cell at your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to summarise this incident, as I understand it, you encountered approximately 10 to 12 soldiers in their early 20s.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They were dressed in a variety of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dressed in the same combat clothing but had slightly different jackets on or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One or two of these gentlemen had an HVO patch on their left shoulder; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on one of their shoulders, left or right shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You yourself did not see any Jokers' patches or insignia on any of these people, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean by "Jokers' patches" skull and cross bones, those are what I saw. Whether they were deemed Jokers' patches, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You yourself did not actually speak with any of these individuals. They declined to engage you in conversation; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And no immediate translation was made to you by Ms. Kolaba of what these individuals were saying amongst themselves, was there?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing directed at the time, no, as they wouldn't engage me in direct conversation, and therefore she didn't translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the one subject about which you testified, and we'll discuss this a little more later in your cross-examination, Major, but the subject of snipers. It's a fact, is it not, that snipers were routinely used by both sides during the war, while you were present in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, I believe that there was one incident where you were attempting to arrange for the repair of damaged electrical transmission lines or distribution lines and the people that were engaged in that work effort actually came under diligent and accurate ABiH sniper fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that both sides were equipped with 7,62-millimetre calibre weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a general rule, that was the weapon which they were equipped with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the ABiH also had, in their inventory, 12,7-millimetre weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I think, sir, that you, as the humanitarian liaison officer for the Vitez area, were well aware that the Grbavica feature, a high-ground village, was regularly used by ABiH snipers to shoot at and actually hit people in the HVO, and civilians too, unfortunately. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that feature was used as a firing point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the Grbavica village is actually on top of a hill, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that's to the north -- pretty much the immediate north and a little west of the BritBat compound at Stara Bila?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's very close. It's the obvious feature to the north of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then on the low ground just to the east of the BritBat compound and to the southeast of Grbavica is the village of Divjak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a milinfosum. I think it's milinfosum 130, dated September the 6th, 1993, which has been produced to us, anyway, in redacted form. I would just like to ask you if you recognise it, and I have a couple of questions based upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has this been exhibited, Mr. Sayers, yet or not or simply handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This was an exhibit in the Blaskic case, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But it hasn't been exhibited so far in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, it has not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It can have a new exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D122/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Major, this appears to be in a format slightly different from the previous milinfosum which we have looked at. Do you recognise this as the format of a so-called combat form or milinfosum or don't you recognise it at all?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell just from the extract here. I honestly couldn't say what it's been taken from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This milinfosum is dated just two days, I believe, before the assault on the Grbavica feature by the HVO, and there's a reference here to two soldiers recently being killed, complaints about constant BiH sniping from the high ground. Were these the kinds of complaints that you heard regularly regarding that feature, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment in time, early September, yes, it was becoming quite frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions about that particular document. One other subject I would like to cover is the Busovaca joint commission. It may have been renamed the Vitez joint commission by the time that you arrived in the theatre, but you were familiar with a joint body for the discussion of issues that arose as a result of the fighting between the two sides; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of such a body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever participate in any of the meetings of this joint commission, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in providing secure transport for members of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the June/July time period of 1993. You were present in the Vitez area when the Muslim forces initiated major offensives in the area of Travnik and Kakanj in the period of time June the 8th to the 12th of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Major, wouldn't it be fair to say that this was a source of great concern to you as a humanitarian officer because of the large numbers of refugees, Croat refugees, that resulted from the military operations being conducted in the area of the city of Travnik and the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly any action which caused an unfortunate reaction in the area of refugees and humanitarian assistance required, one normally went with the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that there were 15 to 20 thousand Croat refugees that had to leave Travnik and the environs of Travnik as a result of the ABiH offensive in the second week of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly a large number. The exact figure, I can't remember. But, yes, a large number of Croat refugees did have to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that about 15.000 refugees had to leave the Kakanj area as a result of a concomitant offensive by ABiH forces being launched in that town?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was briefed about that by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware of separate ABiH offensives being launched in the area of Fojnica to the south of Busovaca in approximately the first week of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And those also resulted in significant numbers of Croat refugees having to leave their homes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly caused a humanitarian requirement to try and get into that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In the Bugojno area, I don't know whether that was in your particular area of responsibility, but you were certainly aware that there was a major ABiH offensive in the Bugojno area July and August of 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't actually get involved in that area. We had the general brief from the company that was in Gornji Vakuf and looked after that area, and so, yes, I was made aware. But as to specific details, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you briefed about the house burnings and lootings that were taking place in the Bugojno area, if you can recall right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this point. It's beyond the scope -- excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to object at this point as beyond the scope of direct. We had nothing to deal with in these areas. We understand we covered a broad area, but still we're getting far afield, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The relevance is, Your Honour, that we're facing Count 1, which is the persecution count, which is the most amorphous count that we face particularly, and I think it's particularly significant that in the area of Central Bosnia, where the Croats are asserted to have been persecuting Muslims, what we are attempting to show, and I think that we've been attempting to show this throughout the course of our cross-examination, that this is really -- and I think the Major agrees with this -- this is a two-way street. It's not a one-way street with the HVO forces having the numerical superiority and the power to impose a small minority. Essentially, you've got even forces, both political -- or both civilian and military, and they are both engaged in internecine fighting in a wide variety of areas, including the areas that the Major talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but he had nothing to do with Bugojno, and that's the point. The other point is this, isn't it? While it may be true, and I think it's accepted that there was misconduct, using that word as neutrally as one can, on both sides, we're still, on the evidence of this witness, left with the shooting up of the convoy, and we've seen that on the video, and the murders in Stupni Do, the three women killed in that vegetable cellar. Now, how does it help your case to say, "Oh, well, the Muslims were doing very much the same sort of thing"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All the background, this has nothing to do with the accused directly because, of course, it's got to be shown that they were in some way involved. But as far as the background of the case, the basic offences, what the Prosecution says, that these incidents occurred, that they amounted to the various crimes they allege, and as far as I see your case, you don't dispute that the incidents occurred, but what you say is, "Oh, well, the Muslims were doing the same." I'm not sure how that really helps you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we clearly do not dispute that events occurred at places such as Stupni Do. I don't think we have tried to dispute that, nor could we. The events occurred. I hope that I will get into this in some further detail with the Major when I actually address Stupni Do, but let me foreshadow that particular subject, since you raised it. Our position is that obviously grave excesses were committed by the troops that were present in that village, but the village was defended. They received advance notice of an impending attack. Notwithstanding that notice, for some inexplicable reason the military authorities in the village decided not to evacuate the civilians, to keep them there, despite receiving a specific order from the war presidency in exile in Dabravine to evacuate them. So the civilians were kept there, and I think that there was some kind of house-to-house fighting that one saw in Ahmici occurred using the same kind of FIBUA tactics. That's our position. Excesses occurred, but during the course of a military operation and in the context of sporadic intercommunal fighting between the two ethnical communities around that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I doubt this witness can help very much about that. No doubt, you can call your own evidence in due course. But as far as Bugojno is concerned, going back to the original question, it seems to me that if you just look at the map, it's out of the area with which this witness was concerned, and all he could do, if he did, was to hear about things. I don't think it's going to assist to go into a lot of detail with this particular witness about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I take your point precisely, Mr. President, and I will move immediately on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Major, in the area with which you were concerned, one of the areas, the Travnik area, you were aware that there were atrocities committed by Muslim forces in the village of Cuklji and Maljina [phoen] in the second week of June 1993; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in the village of Miletici as well, pretty much contemporaneously with your arrival in your area of operations?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that members of your battalion actually themselves witnessed some of these awful events where civilians were killed, Croat civilians in the villages I've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that was the case, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to one of the events about which you did testify, the Convoy of Joy. Were you aware, sir, that on the evening before the fighting actually broke out involving the members of the convoy, and I believe that was June the 11th, 1993, the night before there had been an incident in which artillery was used in Stari Vitez to fire a round that landed in a playground right next to eight children, and they were blown apart and killed as a result of that shell fire?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the numbers killed, but, yes, that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that that incident, along with the incidents of mass exodus from the Croat civilian population in the Travnik area, made the civilians in your area of responsibility absolutely furious?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The local population had been expanded by the Croat population from the Travnik area. There was a steady diversity of the two sides, a polarisation of the two sides. A great deal of animosity had been created.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This convoy, sir, was a purely private convoy; it was not sponsored by any organisation affiliated with the United Nations, was it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it was completely unsponsored and unrecognised by the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I appreciate that the policy of the British Battalion may have changed as a result of this convoy or the incidents that were connected with it, but it is true, is it not, that prior to June the 11th, 1993, it was not within the mandate of the British Battalion to get involved with purely private convoys such as this one?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it certainly wasn't the policy to directly escort non-governmental organisations or unsponsored convoys or, to that degree, any sponsored or UNHCR ones at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We all saw the videotape of the events connected with that convoy, but it is true, is it not, that the drivers of the convoy had been warned that it would be extremely dangerous to drive right through Croat-held territory, especially in the midst of an ABiH offensive immediately to the west?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the convoy were explained the dangers that would happen, on a number of occasions, both crossing the border from Croatia and to -- into Bosnia-Herzegovina, again at Gornji Vakuf, where we had entered the BritBat area. So they had a number of warnings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We saw what I believe were Warrior armoured fighting vehicles actually firing rounds apparently into the air on the videotape, but it's true, is it not, that actually two Croat soldiers were killed by your battalion on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I think it was the Saturday, midmorning, probably nearer midday, when the soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did your regiment ever earn the nickname of "ShootBat" in an article authored by a gentleman by the name of Edward Vulliamy from the Guardian newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we had been given that nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn away from that, sir, to the subject that you dealt with involving the killing of Ms. Dobrila Kolaba. This shooting incident was actually the subject of an investigation that was led by then Captain Whitworth, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he actually led it, but he was involved in gathering information, as the Vitez liaison officer, to pass it back and forward to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be fair to say that he would be in the best position to know what conclusions would be reached regarding that particular shooting incident, more so than you, because he was involved in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if he was involved directly in investigation, then he would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you would therefore defer to Captain Whitworth regarding the results of the investigation and the conclusions that were reached as a result of it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, although I'm unaware of any conclusion reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one question with respect to the mechanism of aid delivery that you facilitated as the liaison officer. As I understand it, sir, humanitarian aid was not actually delivered straight to the civilian population but was actually delivered to a warehouse controlled by nongovernmental organisations such as, for example, Caritas for the Croats or Merhamet for the Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the general method of distributing aid, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to another discrete subject, the small town of Kruscica, just to the south of -- or it's actually the southeast of Vitez. It's fair to say that that town is approximately one kilometre away from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes sir, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's also fair to say that you were aware that the civilian population in Kruscice and the military forces headquartered there actually had a supply route up from the south; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So your access was basically barred from the north, but you don't know what aid, if any, was getting in through the road that came up through the -- from the south, rather?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's right. The track from the south certainly wouldn't be of any use to the large vehicles used by the aid agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You, yourself, gained entry to Kruscice on September the 29th; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you found at that time that the 17th Krajina Brigade, under the leadership of commander Fikret Cuskic, had established a presence in the town; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, you yourself saw a large map in the office of the 325th Brigade commander, Ramiz Dugalic, with arrows showing the points at which the ABiH forces intended to sever the Vitez/Busovaca pocket, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning now to Stari Vitez, sir, in Stari Vitez, it's true that there were combatants mixed in with noncombatants; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There was a unit of the 325th Mountain Brigade in Stari Vitez under the command of Sefkija Dzidic; right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also gave some testimony, Major, concerning the fighting in Stari Vitez and your view of it as a gradual process of attrition designed to wear down the will of the opposing forces. Isn't that the objective of every siege that has ever been embarked upon since the dawn of time?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the aim appeared to be containment and general wearing down of their military capability, but never to any real conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Didn't the ABiH forces surrounding the Vitez/Busovaca pocket have precisely the same objective?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would appear so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that in your discussions with commander Dzidic in Stari Vitez, he had actually told you that the residents of Stari Vitez had made their own decision to stay and fight to protect their own homes rather than leave that part of the town?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was generally not too -- too concerned with the military aspects of what was happening within Stari Vitez. My main concern was the humanitarian side. But I was given the impression that people wished to stay, as they tended to say they had nowhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. You also testified about linkage demands made by both sides concerning the provision of humanitarian aid. That was a general tactic that was actually used by both sides, wasn't it, not just by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was widespread and very common.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, you perceived that the local commanders on both sides, both the Muslim side and the Croat side, routinely used their own injured persons as pawns to obtain military concessions; right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it happened in Nova Bila, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But it happened on both sides; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my personal experience, I can only say that it happened in -- to me, personally -- on an evacuation from Nova Bila. It could well have been used by both sides. I'm sure it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On page 5 of your April 1997 statement, you said that the local commanders of both sides would use their own injured and starving as pawns in their military games. You wouldn't disagree with that now, today, would you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As widespread across the Lasva Valley, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember one incident in August of 1993 when you visited a morgue in Zenica in an attempt to locate the body of a 7-year-old Croat boy who had been killed and that you undertook this effort at the request of his parents?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir, Marko Bralo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you went to the mortuary, you found bodies laid out, covered very respectfully with white sheets, but were told that all of those bodies were Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were also informed that there was a separate mortuary for Croats located in a different building; right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to raise these memories again, Major, but you were absolutely appalled by what you saw when you went to visit that building, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you were told to help yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually bodies had been thrown into that room in a random fashion, one on top of another; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would say there were approximately 30, 35 bodies, naked and stacked one on top of each other, in various states of decay, in a non-refrigerated room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that resulted in a complaint to the ICRC by you, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On the subject of the Nova Bila hospital about which you testified yesterday, that was one of two Croat medical facilities in the Lasva Valley; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Nova Bila hospital specifically was what you referred to as a battle trauma hospital that had about 120 makeshift beds that had been -- that resulted from pushing pews in a church together; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There were makeshift, and they would utilise the pews to maximise the space, the bed space that they could get.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that facility had the ability to accommodate about 120 seriously wounded people; right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was the approximate figure I was given by the administrators in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, unfortunately, the facility was usually full, in your experience, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, unfortunately, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In the hospital, you came across people suffering from precisely the same kind of gunshot wounds and battle-trauma wounds that you saw amongst the people in Stari Vitez; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Including women and children?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And these traumatic injuries were caused by gunfire or shellfire aimed at Croat-held positions by ABiH forces; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the conclusion I came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You found the surgical facilities, or your medical colleagues in your battalion found the surgical facilities very rudimentary and were actually rather appalled by the primitive conditions that confronted you there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I took the commanding officer of the mobile surgical team up there to see if he could assist, and that was his general impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you visited there, you actually found operations being performed in the basement, as well as in the side rooms, in these primitive conditions that you've talked about; right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two other -- or two final questions in this regard. You did attempt to evacuate 55 wounded people from the Nova Bila hospital to Kiseljak with the ultimate aim of putting them into helicopters so that they could be flown to obtain emergency medical treatment; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We undertook a number of these, I can't remember the exact number, how many times we did it; three or four, maybe, approximately. It was always 50-or-so people each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: These are people who were extremely seriously ill?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The criteria was they couldn't receive the medical attention they required in Nova Bila, and it was either life-threatening or permanently damaging.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The evacuation of these people was actually held up by the ABiH side as they tried to negotiate for collateral concessions in other areas; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evacuations were held up on numerous occasions, and that was one of the excuses that was given, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the battle trauma hospital was marked with big red crosses?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember one large red cross. I can't remember exactly how many there were, but I do distinctly remember one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And notwithstanding that red cross, and notwithstanding the fact that the facility was in a church, it nonetheless came under ABiH artillery fire in September of 1993, and you were actually in the facility when it was hit three times by shells; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It blew out all of the windows and actually killed two people; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly blew the windows out. As to if people were killed there, right now -- I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On the subject of ABiH artillery assets, we have many milinfosums that we can go through, but I don't think that it's necessary, Major, because there is no question that artillery fire was regularly targeted at Vitez and at the Croat enclave by ABiH artillery; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In connection with the artillery fire aimed into the town of Vitez, you had absolutely no idea what the targets were, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From -- personally, me, no, I could not say what they were going for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to the Grbavica assault on the 8th of September, isn't it true that your colleagues made the training film comment, because they actually saw standard FIBUA -- Fighting In Built-Up Areas -- techniques employed in the effective assault of that feature?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think the comment arose because it -- from a professional soldier's point of view, it was a professional military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. There's no question, given the fact that the Grbavica feature and the village buildings were used as concealment spots for sniper fire, there's no doubt in your mind that that was a legitimate military target, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To clear military out of an area, then obviously you have to go into wherever they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Major, the question was put in a very tendentious way, so perhaps you would like to think about it. What was suggested was that you had no doubt in your mind; well, that's for you to say. But the question really was, was Grbavica a genuine military target? Can you help on that?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a professional point of view, to secure access across the road so it was not overlooked by an opposing force, then yes, it would be a military objective to take enemy off that hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I did not mean to put the question in a tendentious way, but looking at it on the computer, it certainly appears that way. Thank you very much for clearing that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You mentioned an exclusion zone around the BritBat compound at Stari Bila. That was a 500-metre circular exclusion zone in which no fighting at all was supposed to occur; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it was four or five hundred metres. An agreement I believe was reached with the commanding officer and the local military forces that the two sides should not engage in sniper activities at each other because to do so, they had to shoot over the top of our camp, and we were taking minor casualties because of the fall of shot, so we tried to have an exclusion zone where no sniping would take place. It was generally observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to one of the final subjects that I would like to cover, and that is the visit that you made to the village of Stupni Do at the end of October 1993. Is it not the case that Stupni Do was actually in the area of responsibility of NordBat, the Scandinavian battalion?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, the Norwegian battalion were starting to take over the responsibility for that area. They arrived two or three weeks beforehand, I think, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware from your briefings by the military intelligence cell at your battalion, sir, that there had been some significant fighting in the Stupni Do area immediately before the assault on Stupni Do that occurred on October the 23rd, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had been briefed that fighting was in that area, but I can't remember specifics at that particular time, no. But fighting was certainly going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would just like to see if I can jog your memory with a milinfosum prepared by your regiment on the 22nd of October, 1993, milinfosum number 177.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D123/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The passage of this to which I would like to draw your attention is a short one on page 2, sir, right up at the top, concerning a conversation between General Merdan and one of your colleagues. Were you aware that an attack on Kopljari was undertaken as a punitive action and did not supposedly presage a more general attack on the town of Vares itself? Does this jog your memory at all?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm afraid it doesn't, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No problem. Were you aware that actually a more general attack was launched on Vares by the ABiH in the first two days of November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall that there was fighting in that area, around that area, but as to specifics, sir, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you ever instructed or informed by anyone on the ABiH side or otherwise that evacuation instructions had, in fact, been issued just two days before the military action at Stupni Do on the 23rd of October, 1993, and that those instructions had been issued by the president of the war presidency in exile immediately to the south, the Muslim authorities, and specifically by Mrs. Mervana Hadzimotezic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly talk that a withdrawal had been discussed, but I can't recall by who or to who.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that if military units are given advance notice of an impending assault and that the object of that assault contains a significant civilian population, it is their duty to make sure that the civilians are evacuated so that they aren't hurt?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could depend on a lot of factors, and I don't think I could really comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In response to one of the Judges' questions, you testified, I believe, that it looked to you as if one of the three ladies in the basement identified in the photographs that you covered had had her throat cut, but I'd just like to put it to you, isn't it true that she actually received a 7,62-millimetre round in her neck and that the blood had run down her neck to make it look as if the throat had been cut?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could well have been, sir. Obviously, the light was very poor, we were using torches, we weren't allowed to move the bodies, but that was my general observation at the time. If that's what's been found, then I don't object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Finally, sir, isn't it true that you never actually met Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you yourself don't have any specific factual knowledge of what kind of political influence or power, if any, he had in the Lasva Valley generally or in Busovaca specifically; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, not personally, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Major, thank you very much indeed. I don't have any further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. Before Mr. Sayers concludes his examination, I did want to interrupt some minutes ago, but I would ask Mr. Sayers to put to the witness the conclusions of Mr. Whitworth concerning the shooting of the interpreter, because I think there's perhaps either a -- well, let's assume good-faith confusion on the issue between. Mr. Whitworth testified there was an HVO commission which said that an ABiH soldier had run into an HVO position, fired the shot, and ran back across the confrontation line, which Mr. Whitworth said was within the realm of impossibility that that would have happened. Once again, the question was put to this witness without showing the document or putting the conclusions in front of him, and I would ask either Mr. Sayers to provide that document to him or provide it to us so that we can redirect on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I hadn't understood that myself. Were you referring to a document? I thought you were referring to Mr. Whitworth's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's precisely what I was referring to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then how can this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to re-examine about it, Mr. Scott, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And if the Court wants, I can address the point that was made by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Major Bower. My name is Goran Mikulicic. Together with my colleague, Mr. Kovacic, I act as Defence counsel for Mr. Mario Cerkez. Major Bower, at the very outset I should like to ask you about the following: You said in your statement that you met Mr. Cerkez on several occasions. Can you describe the circumstances to us? When and where did this happen, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meetings were not arranged, they were normally -- because I would be looking for either Captain Whitworth or meeting a humanitarian aid person and would be in the same location as Mr. Cerkez, and that was the sum extent of the meetings. It was the same time, same place, no prearranged meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Mr. Cerkez's liaison officer was at that time? Did you talk to that person?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only liaison officer which I spoke to in that area was Darko Gelic, sir, which I believe is the Hotel Vitez liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So that was Mr. Blaskic's liaison officer; right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Major Bower, do you know how the Vitez Brigade was set up, the one that was headed by Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the other units that were operating in the town and municipality of Vitez at the time when you were there, in addition to the Vitez Brigade, that is?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are purely HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm referring to the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of individual subunits within that area. It was not really my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in your testimony that you also encountered HOS units. Is it correct that you could have seen these units throughout the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. I did see them throughout the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you saw them in Vitez itself?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier on in your testimony that these units were well equipped, that they had good weapons, and that in this way they differed from the usual recruits of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's an accurate summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that they drove western cars; in addition to others, Volkswagen Golfs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is one car which particularly sticks in my mind about this particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Major Bower, are you aware of the fact that this vehicle, the VW Golf, was manufactured in Sarajevo, only about 40 kilometres away from the area that you were in?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I was unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to a different subject. You mentioned, Major Bower, that on one occasion you saw a HIP helicopter. Is it correct that this was a white helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see any insignia in terms of its military affiliation on it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Major Bower, do you recall that at that time above all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was a no-fly zone that was carried out by the International Community?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I was aware that there was a no-fly zone trying to be imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time, helicopter flights called medevac were being carried out and they had to be reported to UNPROFOR? This referred to medical evacuations.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unaware of that, but it would seem reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When we are mentioning the provision of medical supplies, and that is what you were involved in, you negotiated, for the largest part, with Mr. Santic, the mayor of Vitez about this. He was a representative of the civilian authorities, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Santic was a member of the civilian authorities, but I only was involved in trying to get aid through Gacice. I didn't speak to him about getting aid into Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In addition to Mr. Santic, you talked to Gelic, Mr. Blaskic's liaison officer whom we mentioned earlier on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So your contacts on the provision of medical assistance actually took place only in the Hotel Vitez, where Mr. Blaskic's headquarters was; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Major Bower, you know that Mr. Cerkez's headquarters was at the Vitez cinema?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever seek any kind of permit related to your work, in terms of providing medical supplies, in that particular building?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Major Bower, a few minutes ago you talked to my colleague Mr. Sayers about Kruscica and the provision of medical assistance to Kruscica. I would like to ask the usher to show Z2624 that was tendered yesterday. That's a map where you marked the village of Kruscica, so I have a few questions in that respect. Major, you marked the village of Kruscica with the number "4", didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please, could you show us on the map the road that you used for providing medical aid, bringing it into Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would say it was either this one here [indicates] or the one to the east, and I can't honestly remember at this time now. It was one of the two roads going south.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I saw it right on the screen, you showed the eastern road leading to Kruscica. Right?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two roads here [indicates]. I can't remember now, after some seven years, which of the roads it was. Obviously, just going off this small-scale map now, it was one of those roads to enter. I can't remember which one, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you always used one of these two roads?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, sir, there was only one road available to enter Kruscica. I can't remember which of those two roads it was, but it was always the same road to try and enter Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Major Bower, why it was not possible to enter Kruscica on the other road, because it is obvious from the map that you can get into Kruscica by taking two roads that are of the same category, at least according to the markings on the map. What was the reason why you could not take the other road to Kruscica? Rather, why did you not use the other road to get to Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can remember, one road was either blocked, unsuitable, or unsafe. There was only one road, otherwise obviously we would have used and utilised whatever method we could. But there was only one method of gaining entry into Kruscica, but I can't honestly remember the reason now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember that there was a line of delineation along this road between the HVO and the BH army, and that practically went down the road?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember at this moment in time now, I'm sorry. It's just too far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. I won't bother you any longer. I won't try to jog your memory endlessly. Yesterday, you spoke about what you called discriminatory artillery fire, and today you agreed that this kind of fire actually prevailed in the Lasva River Valley, notably in Vitez, from both sides, from both armies, from both parties to the conflict. I'm going to ask you about an incident that was referred to just a while ago and you said that you remembered, when at the school playground in Vitez, on the 10th of June, ten children were killed by such discriminatory fire. Major Bower, I carefully looked at all the milinfosums and ECMM reports, but this event was not described anywhere. Do you have any comment with regard to that?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't produce the military information summaries. We did not, as a matter of course, from what I recall, log every single incident which resulted in casualties. Obviously, the military information summaries would just be too big to deal with. I remember an incident where children were killed or injured and around a play area. The exact date, I can't recall, but I know that an incident like that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I shall remind you, Major Bower, that at that time in June, there was also an incident that occurred with the Convoy of Joy. You mentioned to us that this convoy had been stopped at the so-called T-crossroads by Novi Travnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly where it was stopped at each time throughout the Lasva Valley, but it tended to be at major crossroads on its route through the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Major, I was referring to the most important incident that occurred when there was shooting and when people were actually shot. Will you agree with me that that was at the T-crossroads by Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that specific incident did happen at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So that is outside the municipality of Vitez, it is in the territory of the municipality of Novi Travnik; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual municipality or brigade boundaries again weren't particularly my concern.
