utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic. It's 11.00. Would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Major Bower, several additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I believe that on the map which we had been talking about -- it's still on the ELMO; this is Exhibit 2624 -- Major, you marked on this map the location of Grbavica as number 6. In your testimony you said that you personally observed the combat operation in the Grbavica area from the vantage point of your base in Bila; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I observed the start and some of the period of fighting, but not the whole battle. As you can appreciate, there were times when obviously we had to take cover, and obviously only what I could see from the base itself, so the forward-facing slope of the houses and the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Major, the hill and the houses you just mentioned were part of the village of Stara Bila; isn't that correct, and that was marked with a circle above the number 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Major, this location is due north from the secondary road leading to the town of Vitez which has also been marked on the map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's northwest of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Another location, which is to the southeast of that road, is named Divjak. Can you see it on the map?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Major, it is not in dispute that these are two separate locations which are about two kilometres from each other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking Divjak to Vitez, or Divjak to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We're talking Divjak and Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say under two kilometres, but yes, 1,500 metres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, you spent a fair amount of time in Vitez and in the municipality of Vitez. Do you know whether, during the conflict which took place in this area, about 700 citizens of Croatian nationality were killed and an additional 800 wounded throughout this period of hostilities? Are you familiar with these numbers?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not familiar with exact numbers of casualties, alive or dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Major, let's start with the last questions. Looking at Exhibit 2624, I just want to be very careful about this. Looking at the area generally around number 6, the British Battalion camp was in Stari Bila; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that's, in fact, what's reflected by, if you will, the smaller circle above the handwriting "Grbavica"; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's the approximate location of where I think the camp was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So not the village that was being attacked, but, in fact, the camp, the British Battalion camp itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look, in fact, on this --

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- they were almost one and the same. They were very close to one another. Certainly the houses in Stari Bila which were attacked, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly. If you're looking to the southwest from the British Battalion camp, you're looking at a forward-facing slope that would run along, if you would, the spine -- roughly along this oblong shape that you've put on the map; is that correct? At least in part?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could see some of the houses, but obviously the majority of the actual village was on the other side of the hill, which wasn't able to be seen from the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. But the fighting that you've described to us, albeit immediately -- even outside the boundaries, and they even came into your house, you testified yesterday -- was in that southwesterly direction from the camp overall?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, and to be clear, in reference to counsel for Mr. Cerkez's questions, the name "Divjak," you see that on the map; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see anywhere on this map, in that particular locale, the name "Grbavica"?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only that's been handwritten in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did you have occasion during your tour in Bosnia, sir, to find that there were areas that sometimes had more than one reference, or there might be subparts of a broader populated area?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there were places where they were referred to differently depending on which ethnic group you spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Concerning the lines of authority to gain access to such places as Stari Vitez, sir, you did not find that confusing, did you? You knew to go to Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Concerning counsel's questions whether you were ever asked in your prior statements or testimony about Mr. Kordic, when you were interviewed in April of 1997, do you even know if Mr. Kordic was in custody at that time or not?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I had no idea, in April of 1997, as to what the state of anything which was happening with our tour in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mentioned in connection with the victim and a doctor being, in Mr. Sayers' term, being smuggled out of Stari Vitez. Assuming that's a fair characterisation, why did you find it necessary to, quote, "smuggle" someone out of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular incident, we had been expressly told that no one was to enter or leave Stari Vitez. The doctor had told me that this man -- I think he was 50, 55 years old -- would die if he didn't get to Zenica hospital. I tried to get the ICRC or UNHCR involved. They refused because of the situation at the time. I had to make a decision at that time on the ground. The doctor agreed to accompany the casualty in the back of the vehicle. It was the only thing that I could do to try and save a life. Unfortunately, the man died sometime later in Zenica hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Concerning the HIP helicopter, in the nightly briefings that you've testified about, do you recall any incident or any time when there was discussion that helicopter flights into the Lasva Valley had been cleared by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally can't recall whether there were or weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But the information available to you was that this helicopter was landing in a HVO-controlled area, and Mr. Dalic [sic] had made comments to you about it bringing in supplies?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had been reported to us that -- I think it was by Darko Gelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Gelic"; excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that it had brought in some -- I think it was special equipment, or equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Concerning access to Kruscica, sir, whether or not there may have been some other road from the south, is it nonetheless the case that you were repeatedly obstructed by the HVO from coming into the village of Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It wasn't practical to try and attempt from the south; to do so, we'd have probably had to go to Gornji Vakuf and try and enter that far south. It would have taken hours, over a road which was unproven, not tarmacked. It was just -- it was not practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The visit by the mayor of Vitez, Mr. Santic, to the roadblock at Kruscica, is it correct, sir, that Mr. Santic came there for something approximating 20 minutes, perhaps a half hour?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe a little longer. No more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have any information, in fact, or an assessment of whether Mr. Santic, in fact, himself had any real desire to accommodate or accomplish your access into Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an attempt made, but it waned very early on. To me, it appeared he was going through the motions of being seen to attempt to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was your assessment of Mr. Santic, in terms of your working with him, about his basic attitudes towards assisting you and the humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't a diligent approach. Generally, it would always result in wanting something in return for whatever we wanted to do. There was always a quid pro quo about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me be blunt: Was Mr. Santic someone that you enjoyed dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt that I couldn't trust him, and that I wouldn't get the assistance that I needed for humanitarian mission, what I was trying do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Convoy of Joy, the drivers had been warned that it was a possibly -- quite likely, perhaps -- a dangerous situation. Did you have an understanding that this relief convoy was intended for Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had been briefed on it as soon as it started to form up in Croatia, and its intended destination. It was obviously of great importance to us, so we kept up to date on it throughout the days, and certainly we knew that they had been briefed not to enter, and its ultimate destination and its composition, number of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you recall sir, that the humanitarian situation in Tuzla at that time was severe?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that particular time, there was a subunit of our battalion based in Tuzla, with a liaison officer, which reported back daily as to the situation from the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In short, sir, these drivers, although warned, persisted in trying to get humanitarian aid to Tuzla, and many of them paid with their lives?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the persistence was there, and a number did die.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you aware of any conclusions that your colleague, Mr. Whitworth, came to concerning the murder of your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personal conclusions, or conclusions of a formed body?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Any conclusions that he came to or discussed with you.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was general discussion amongst the liaison officers as to what could have happened. It was believed it had come from an HVO position. But a formed opinion, I am unaware of any result of any -- any formed body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you ever aware -- sorry, Your Honour, I'm trying to wait for the translation. Did it ever come to your attention that some HVO group or commission had concluded that your interpreter had been shot by a member of the ABiH forces who had crossed the confrontation line, entered into a house otherwise under HVO control, fired the shot that killed your interpreter, left the house, went back across the confrontation line, all without being otherwise detected or harmed? Was that proposition ever put to you, or did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall hearing in that explicit detail. I had heard a number of -- through a number of discussions with other military liaison officers what the various permutations of the incident were, but I'm unaware up until today of any formed opinion as to what actually happened at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you agree with Mr. Whitworth's assessment that that explanation is within the realm of the impossible?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I agree. I don't think it's very helpful. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to Exhibit 2624, the map, please, the reference to area 1, at the time -- I'm sorry. At the time you marked that on the map, the circle and number 1, did you have any contemporaneous documents or other maps or sketches of the area available to you in trying to determine this location?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the time you were stopped by these troops west of Busovaca, did you at that time attempt to make a precise record of your location at the time that these soldiers were threatening to kill you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On return to the BritBat location, I would have mentioned it to the military information officer where I was, the general area. But I have no personal record of exactly where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But is it fair to say, Major, that this large area marked as number 1 is more or less a general approximation simply indicating an area in the mountains west of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's a general area where I think I was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In contrast, for instance, to your rather more precise markings concerning number 2 and number 3?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There have been several references to FIBUA, fighting in built-up areas. Are you familiar with that military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it part of the accepted military practice or part of that doctrine that fighting in built-up areas allows the deliberate targeting and killing of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For -- for our army, for my army, no, the Geneva Convention rules have to apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what you repeatedly saw happening in Stari Vitez in terms of the victims that you were taking out, is it fair to say that what you saw and encountered was the deliberate targeting of civilians in a number of instances?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would say it was indiscriminate over a protracted period of time, resulting in the death and injury of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apart from the sniper fire, the other weapon that we talked about in terms of these fire-extinguisher bombs, did you find that again to be a weapon that was used indiscriminately against the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was indiscriminate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The attack on Grbavica, when you commented this was a professional military operation, sir, were you commenting on the manner of its execution, or the way that the civilians in that town were treated?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a comment on the overall tactical plan, how the fighting started and how it progressed at the lowest level, seeing the soldiers in combat. It was a professional observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, in terms of the manner in which the troops were disposed, the disposition of forces, the way they advanced, the way they conducted themselves?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I saw, sir, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that again, fighting in a built-up area does not include the cleansing of Muslim civilians out of their homes?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in the small area which we could observe and had some limited control of, we were able to gather the Muslim population together and evacuate them. We did that because we feared that they would be resultant casualties if we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact what you saw was that the Muslim houses were burned, destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, this is all leading. Mr. Scott, I must remind you you are reexamining. You have been going for more than a quarter of an hour, and it is time to let the witness go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will conclude, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You recall, sir, just to conclude with this, that after this attack on Grbavica, the Muslim houses were looted and Bosnian Croat families were moved into those houses, the ones that survived?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded and you are released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as I know, the next witness is outside and the usher will bring him in, but I haven't been able to go outside and check since the break. Ms. Somers will be taking the next witness. There will be a change of counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may it please the Court, two minor things. First, there was some insinuation that the use of a word that I used in cross-examination was somehow improper, the word "smuggle". That actually came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you needn't trouble about this. I mean if there were allegations of impropriety, we would take them seriously. Mere forensic hyperbole we take no notice of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very good, Your Honour. Secondly, with respect to this witness, Major or ex-Major Buffini, we've just been given a copy of his proposed -- the outline of his proposed testimony. I would like to draw the Court's attention to page 6, paragraph 31. It appears that we have yet another witness who is going to give some testimony about the Convoy of Joy, once again a subject that has been repeatedly covered and is not covered in the amended indictment, and so at this point I think we would like to make a formal application, if we may, to preclude any further evidence on this subject. It's simply not relevant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll deal with it when we come to the paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat, Mr. Buffini.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: It's Michael Leslie Buffini, and 18th of November, 1956.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: An investment advisor working in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you employed or were you in some capacity in the former Yugoslavia, and could you please give the time frames?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I was employed in the former Yugoslavia between the 15th of January of 1993 and the 12th of July of the same year.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Prior to your deployment in the former Yugoslavia, had you been in the military, and if so, could you describe your jobs?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes. I joined the Royal Marines in February of 1977 as a recruit, commissioned during training as an officer, and had a series of jobs from 1978 until '88, first of all working in Malta as a troop command, then in Cyprus with the United Nations in Dhekalia and Nicosia, then went back to the United Kingdom, trained as a mortar officer and deployed for four and a half months in Northern Ireland, and then had a series of jobs as recruiting for the Royal Navy, as staff officer, recruitment -- sorry, not a recruiting, a training officer's job at the commando training centre, working as a staff officer in the Falkland Islands, and then working with Commander In Chief Fleet in Northwood, where I was responsible for Royal Marines deployed throughout the globe, mainly working for the navy on board ships responsible for nuclear security and other types of jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you, during your period in the military, did you leave the military and rejoin, if I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes. In 1988, I left and spent two years working as an investment advisor in Hong Kong, before I was asked to rejoin in 1990 for another five-year period.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What assignment were you given when you rejoined in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: In 1990, I was assigned a job as the training of systems team in the Royal Marines pool, so another staff officer's job.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you describe the period of deployment when you went from the U.K. and your arrival in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: In December of '92, I was asked if I would work with the United Nations in the former Yugoslavia and deployed as a U.K. liaison -- OC liaison officer and watchkeeper in January, so the 15th of January flew into Split and worked from Divulje there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher, please, to present a map, actually a couple of maps, the first of which is in black and white from the Croatian atlas, Z2612,9. If the usher would be kind enough to place that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you indicate, if it's clear to you, indicate to the Court the location of Divulje and the places to which you first deployed?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Divulje is located here just west of Split [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate on this map where the boundary between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is? Is it in some way delineated?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, it's delineated quite clearly with a line up here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would just like to confirm something. You are no longer with the Royal Marines. Did you leave for any particular reason?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes. I was medically invalided from the Royal Marines because I have osteoarthritis in both knees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Turning to the map, once you arrived and were stationed in the Divulje barracks, what were your principal roles?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I had two principal roles. The first was as the OC -- the officer commanding the United Kingdom liaison officers, and the second was as a watchkeeper for commando British forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you be able to describe the taskings that would go with these positions, and under whose supervision, and under who your chain of command was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: As part of commando British forces, I worked for Brigadier Andrew Cummings and deployed nine teams of UKLOs around Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That acronym, UKLOs, stands for --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: U.K. liaison officers, sorry. So I deployed the teams and took the decisions as to where they should deploy, based on discussions with Brigadier Cummings and his chief of staff, and made sure that they carried out the duties required from Brigadier Cummings' orders, which is really the gathering of various information about what was happening in both areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have direct links with other units, and if so, could you describe them, please?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Commando British forces worked directly for United Kingdom land forces in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: It was in Salsbury, in Wiltshire, so from their base at Wilton. Commando British forces also had direct links to BritBat based in Vitez, they had direct links with UNPROFOR headquarters in Kiseljak, and commanded other British troops throughout various places in Croatia and also in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have direct links with UNHCR in its various locations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes. Part of my responsibility was a team tasked with working in Metkovic, which is liaison with the UNHCR for convoys and responsibility for passing on information about what was happening with convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where is Metkovic located, in what sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Metkovic is located in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did you task the teams that you had?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I took decisions with the chief of staff and the brigadier about what information was required, and I then ordered my teams to deploy to various locations throughout Bosnia and also in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you describe the type of equipment you were outfitted with?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Each of the nine teams had a soft-skinned truck, which was a Renault Borton 44, which had a maritime INMARSAT telephone system mounted in the back of the truck. We also had GPS global positioning navigation system. We had laptop computers with fax/modems and HF radio systems in the truck as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you describe your role in relation to Brigadier Cummings? What was the relationship? What were you to do for the brigadier?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: We were the eyes and ears of the brigadier, so we were tasked to gather information about what was happening in the various locations, to make sure that we were not surprised by events that were happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At the beginning of February 1993, did you find yourself going to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes. I was tasked to provide two teams to work in Busovaca with the newly-formed Busovaca joint commission, and I tasked Captain Mike Robison and Tom Major to work with the team based in Busovaca. I went up to have discussions about their deployment and what they should be doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was their role to be?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Their role was to act as a communications link and security advice to the European Community Monitoring Commission, the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What were conditions like in Busovaca at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Busovaca was in what I would probably call a real state of conflict. Travel was very difficult because of the roadblocks, checkpoints. We were shot upon on numerous occasions, so a very hostile environment to work within.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have adequate protection in your vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: No. This was something I became quite concerned about, because one of my teams had been shot at and had a round pass about a metre behind the back of their cab, where the driver and the officer were sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I took the teams off deployment until we had confirmation that we could get some armoured support, because I refused to allow the teams to operate within that environment without some armoured protection. So in a meeting with Jeremy Fleming, I insisted that the teams did not deploy until we had armoured support.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the result of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Within, I think, two days, we had armoured support provided by the British Battalion in Vitez, which was authorised by UNPROFOR headquarters in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Going back for a moment to your duties as watchkeeper while you were in Split, could you define what a watchkeeper does?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: A watchkeeper really sifts information coming in from radio reports and telephones, so I'm the first point of contact for ComBritFor. I log those details that are coming in and then take decisions as to who should respond or who should be called in to respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What is route triangle?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Route triangle was the name given to a road between Tomislavgrad and Prozor which was being developed and graded by the Royal Engineers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher at this time to distribute Z2618,2. On the ELMO, please, yes. I'm sorry, our signal is not showing. I'm not sure whether the Court is getting a projection on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is there something that we could do about that or should we attempt to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just keep going. We'll try to get something done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We'll ultimately return to this exhibit, but if you can describe what a route triangle is and its importance to your work.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Route triangle was the connection from Croatia into Central Bosnia, where the British Battalion were working, and it was probably the only route that stayed open whereby we had access from Split, from ComBritFor, into Central Bosnia. To start off with, it was very much a mountain track, which was then upgraded to sort of a dirt road which covered the distance between Tomislavgrad and Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able, by way of description and looking at this map that everyone has in front of himself, to give the parameters -- if you're familiar with this map, why, and if you are, can you give a description of the route so the Court can follow it? And if you would care to get up, perhaps, and point it out.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: The map was the one I used when testifying against Colonel Blaskic or General Blaskic. I've indicated Prozor on the map, which I think most people can see in this area [indicates], and to the west of Prozor there is a route running around a very large lake which is indicated in this area [indicates], and then around down here [indicates], and literally following the edge of this map is where route triangle went further down to Bosnia and Tomislavgrad, and that was route triangle [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In February of 1993, did you witness any movements of HV soldiers going between Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, I personally followed a convoy of between six and eight coaches of -- Croat-identified coaches with HV soldiers in them along route triangle, so I spent about three hours, sat behind these coaches as they drove into Prozor. Once the coaches stopped in Prozor and we overtook them, then went on up to Gornji Vakuf and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. And is Tomislavgrad indicated on this particular map or would you have to refer back to the first map that was in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: It's indicated on the first map, not on this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll try to get it back just so that you can pinpoint it and discuss distances. Again, we're a bit, I think, disabled by the screen. If you are able to point out the location of Tomislavgrad that would catch the attention or give some indicator where it is on the map.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: In relation to Split [indicates], Tomislavgrad is up beyond the border between Croatia and Bosnia and, on this map, is indicated right on the right-hand edge. So that is Tomislavgrad in Bosnia-Herzegovina [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In terms of time, if you know, to go from, let's say, a point called Sinj, S-i-n-j, in Croatia, which is also indicated on the same map, to Tomislavgrad, could you give an approximate time frame, travelling over land?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: On a good day, somewhere between 40 minutes to an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How were you able to determine that the soldiers whom you saw were, in fact, HV soldiers, Republic of Croatia soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: There were two instances. The first one was through the fact that the coaches were Croatian vehicles, in the sense of their number plates, their license plates were Croatian, and the second was that the soldiers' insignia was very much "HV" as opposed to "HVO", and we had been used to seeing those and had been given recognition sort of lessons from our intelligence officer in ComBritFor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The soldiers were going towards Prozor. Were they also headed towards Tomislavgrad? Were there two separate identifications you made of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: There were two separate identifications. The first was when we followed the soldiers in the coach from Tomislavgrad to Prozor, and the second identification was a couple of days after that when we were coming back from Vitez, driving through Prozor, we saw six to eight coaches again parked just north of Prozor with a lot of wounded soldiers wearing HV uniforms and wearing the insignias of HV soldiers, battle weary, bandaged, sort of lying on the grass, very tired, getting ready to board the buses, which were Croatian buses, to come back, we assume, through the Tomislavgrad area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You personally saw this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, I personally saw this, witnessed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who is Gus Bryden?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Gus Bryden is a mercenary I met in Trogir, an ex Royal Marine, whom I spent about an hour having conversations with about his activities as a mercenary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, but where is Trogir?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Trogir is west of Divulje barracks, about 5 kilometres west of Divulje barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: In Croatia, on the coastline.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Gus Bryden had been working with the HV in Croatia, training soldiers of the HV to go into conflict in and around the Prozor area. He had also been working around the Zadar area, actually fighting with his son, who is also a mercenary, around the Prozor area and Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you curious about the deployment of Croatian soldiers in the Prozor area, which is in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: We were very curious, because again this was something we had been asked to find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: By ComBritFor, by Andrew Cummings, his staff, and chief of staff and the intelligence cell. And we specifically asked him if the soldiers he was training were conscripts, which he confirmed, and he also confirmed that they were fighting in Bosnia around the Prozor area and not just restricted to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there a military training camp that you observed on the route to Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: We identified a training establishment or a camp just south of Sinj, which is in Croatia, before you come to the border. And we had identified this on several occasions as a -- as a used training camp for the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe that the video is available, and if in fact the map that has Sinj on there were convenient, if you could point it out.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: It's sort of northeast of Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And can -- fine. Are you able to -- I know Prozor is not on this particular map, but are you able to give a general indication of where Prozor would be and where Tomislavgrad is now?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Prozor -- well, Tomislavgrad is, as I say, over on this this area here [indicates], and then Prozor much further north -- northeast.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. This training camp that you observed, did you observe it again?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: We observed it on a regular basis while we were travelling backwards and forwards between Split and Vitez. One incident, we saw that the camp was full of soldiers, lots of trucks, lots of coaches, and was obviously very much in use as a training establishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would this have been in February or March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then what happened? What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Most other observations, that I observed that it was empty. But while I was watchkeeping after having seen it being used, subsequent reports coming in showed that it was empty, that the troops had actually been deployed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you received any reports of actual fighting in Bosnia during that interim period between seeing troops at Sinj and then seeing the camp empty?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: The conflict at that time was ongoing, and on a daily basis we were receiving reports that fighting between Muslims and -- sort of Croats, Bosnian and -- Bosnian Croats, certainly around the Prozor area, on a daily basis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was an injury of an HVO soldier reported to you, and can you describe the injury?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I was watchkeeping and received a report from the Royal Engineers on route triangle, from one of their bases, that a coach carrying HV soldiers had had an incident where a soldier playing with a grenade had let the grenade off and had damaged himself, so he had blown himself --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Was this accident in Bosnia, or was it in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: No, it was in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did you do about it, if anything? What could you do?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I was asked to provide a helicopter evacuation from the helicopter flight based at Divulje, and I refused on the grounds that we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker speak a little more slowly, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I was asked to provide helicopter evacuation but declined on the grounds that it was not part of our remit in providing humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was some assistance ultimately rendered to this soldier?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: No. Not from the United Nations troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you personally follow a convoy of -- sorry, a group of coaches carrying Croatian soldiers into Bosnia? And if we've covered this in another of the incidents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Brigadier Cummings ask you to become involved in what was known as the Busovaca joint commission at the beginning of March of '93?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I was tasked to deploy to Busovaca full time and to provide a higher level of military support to the Busovaca joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just to clarify rank, you were what rank in the Marines, and how was that accommodated to fit the scheme in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I was a captain, Royal Marines, which is the paid equivalent rank of an army major. Normally, when Royal Marines are working with the army, we are promoted to what is known as a local high rank, which was major. So I became a local major.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you to deal with any particular individuals, or what were your tasks, primarily, on the Commission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Tasks of the Busovaca joint commission had been predetermined with two primary people, which was Franjo Nakic from the HVO and Dzemal Merdan from the BiH, with their representatives of local commanders. Our responsibility was to investigate points of conflict arising between each of the sides, to mediate, and to try and resolve the issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to distribute Z548,1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please pause between questions and answers, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, looking at this document, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And if you turn to the page which will be the third page -- it will be identified as having the numbers 00475825 on it -- could you describe, please, the identification of Mr. Nakic there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic is described as the deputy HVO Operational Zone, Middle Bosnia. So our interpretation, deputy commander of that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How often did you meet with the commission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: On a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At a fixed time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Normally at 9.00 each morning, providing everybody could be brought in at the correct time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Among your tasks, was the investigation and mediation of complaints included?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, nearly on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What about checkpoint removal?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: That was all part of the ongoing discussions, but our aim was to open the road between Vitez and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there also an aspect about the investigation of alleged atrocities, ethnic cleansing, attacks on villages, harassment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: That became the main issue. On a daily basis, before anything was done, investigation into each of those circumstances would have to be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Approximately 20th March, '93, did you have to move locations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, we moved location from Busovaca to Vitez, in a house next to the British Battalion camp in --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who is Mats Torping, please? I forgot to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Mats Torping started off as the chairman of the Busovaca joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did he remain chairman during your entire time, or did it change?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: No, it changed because of their time in the job, so there were several chairmen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was one of them Henk Morsink?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, Henk Morsink in the latter stages took over as chairman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Once you moved to Vitez, did the role change, and did you take on more responsibility and jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: We found that once we were in Vitez, a much larger area of responsibility came into question, so we were asked to investigate instances on -- outside of the Busovaca valley, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did it extend to essentially the whole Lasva Valley, and did it retain its name as "Busovaca joint commission"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Because it had grown from the Busovaca area to a much larger area, we decided to drop "Busovaca," and it just became known as the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were there any conditions laid down about the degree of authority that the representatives from each side should have?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes. Both General Merdan and Franjo Nakic were required to have the authority to act to circumstances which the Busovaca and the joint commission met on the ground, in providing orders to local commanders and making decisions which were followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you find that to be the case?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Only in Djemal Merdan's case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me; could you again please pause between question and answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did the case turn out to be with Mr. Nakic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic was clearly not able to take any responsibility for deciding things without referring back to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did this cause tension?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: It caused quite a bit of tension within the joint commission, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If Mr. Merdan were unable to make a firm decision, would he come halfway?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Mr. Merdan would make a provisional agreement or authority and then would clarify the position with his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did something occur with artillery going off during a commission meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: In one meeting we had in Vitez, a number of artillery rounds were fired very close by which shook the house, at which point Mr. Merdan reacted very violently against Nakic, asking why the artillery was being fired when we were supposed to be negotiating ceasefires.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was it, then, HVO artillery?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: It was HVO artillery, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you able to identify the type of weapon, the calibre?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Because of the report, we had an indication that it was certainly heavy, between 120 and 150 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there a particular weapon that was suspected of being fired?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: There was a heavy artillery piece that the British troops around Vitez had nicknamed "Big Bertha" which was a heavy artillery piece, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At the time of the firing, was there a ceasefire in place, and if so, what was the result of this incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I believe there was a ceasefire in place, and Mr. Merdan reacted very violently and refused to take any further part in the joint commission meeting until the whole incident had been investigated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many shells were fired by Big Bertha?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I believe there were approximately 10 or 11 shells fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was any investigation undertaken about this firing, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: An investigation was undertaken, but we had no reports coming back of a response as to who or why it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Based on your professional military experience, can you characterise the degree of respect, orders and decisions issued by Colonel Blaskic commanded?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic had a great deal of authority over the troops that we met, the local commanders, and they would not normally react to any incident without his authority, either verbally or written.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did any violations of his orders come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Only one incident, which was during the Convoy of Peace or Convoy of Hope, where some trucks had been taken in the Busovaca area, and when we questioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, for the grounds previously stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the witness going to say that we haven't heard already, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The witness will simply indicate that this is the one time that a violation of an order was reported to him. There is no specific identification of any of the party, but this is a very focused question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, when you referred to a convoy, was it the Convoy of Joy of June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you just clarify what the issue was with Blaskic's order on that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: The local commander, who had hijacked about seven or ten vehicles and was searching them for arms or ammunition, refused to allow the vehicles to go, despite the fact that we had asked and had authority from Colonel Blaskic to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where was this local commander?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: It was just north of Busovaca. I forget the name of the actual village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you go on R & R in April of '93, and if so, did you make any observations just before departure about the presence of helicopters in the area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: There were several incidents of helicopters which we personally cited, or I personally cited, in and around the Vitez and Zenica area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And this would have been the early part of April?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Both the early part of April and also in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was this restricted to one side, or did you see helicopters on both sides?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I saw helicopters on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Generally speaking, were there no-fly restrictions in place, and if so, for what purpose would a helicopter undertake a risk?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: There was a no-fly restriction on the whole of the Central Bosnia area, and the only reason we could see that helicopters would fly into this area was for the resupply of ammunition and evacuating wounded troops out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you describe the general atmosphere in the Lasva Valley when you left for your temporary R & R on or about the 4th of April of '93?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: With the work of the joint commission, we felt that the Lasva Valley had quietened down quite considerably, and there was a semblance of normality returning to the area just prior to my leaving, so most of the conflict had been restricted to very small areas, and we felt quite pleased with the job that we had achieved at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated that the meetings were daily for the commission. Was there any indication at these daily meetings of an attack, an imminent attack, about which you found out when you returned from your leave?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: None at all. We were very surprised -- I was very surprised, when I returned, at the extent of the activity in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I beg your pardon, but I believe that the transcript has stopped. Is there a technical...? Our screens are not moving, so we've stopped at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see. Where did you get to? There was a no-fly restriction?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, and I've moved on well beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any problem with the transcript? There's none that I can see, Your Honour, but I -- my computer is working fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yours is working, but ours isn't. We're stuck at "no-fly restriction." Just wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we just see what the position is, we are going get a transcript, are we, since yours is working? THE REPORTER: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So there's no reason why we couldn't go on, as it were, although we haven't got the transcript ourselves? THE REPORTER: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if the reporter could just read back to me the last question, I would appreciate it, or if somebody could. I'm sorry. I'm told that they cannot move backward on their screen, so I will attempt to just reconstruct the question, repeating myself, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Prior to your departure, having had daily meetings with the joint commission, was there any indication at these daily meetings that an attack of the nature of Ahmici, various attacks about which you became aware when you returned from leave would occur?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: No, there was no indication of any buildup of hostilities, any buildup of forces and, in fact, we felt we had done a pretty good job with the joint commission in calming the whole situation down in the Lasva Valley prior to my departure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was that shock shared -- excuse me. Was that surprise shared by other international organisations and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, all of the organisations of BritBat, UNPROFOR, and even the UNHCR agencies were all surprised by what had happened during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Mario Cerkez -- sorry, I'll wait. Did Mario Cerkez come to play a role on the commission during this time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, he did, as the representative of HVO troops in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Generally, if you can characterise the attitude of the members of the BiH, or some of the members, towards Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Some of the other local commanders of the BiH were openly, in my view, openly hostile towards the presence of Mario Cerkez at the meetings, to such a point that I used to sit with an armed -- loaded pistol in my belt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were questions posed to Mr. Cerkez by the commission as to the reasons for the ceasefire violations, and if so, what types of answers were offered?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: We asked, on numerous times, why violations had happened, and on most instances where the questions were directed at Mario Cerkez, the response was very flippant, detracting, and normally answered in the sense of another question or allegation of other atrocities against HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In connection with the question posed about who perpetrated Ahmici, do you recall Mr. Cerkez's answer?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: I recall a response from him that he actually accused the BiH of perpetrating the act themselves on the grounds that it put the HVO in a very bad light and curried favour with the BiH with UNPROFOR and other organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the BiH representatives to such responses?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Pure derision. It was a ludicrous statement, and both the BiH and ourselves, as the British forces, ECMM, felt the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Ms. Somers. I would like to ask the witness something. He said that the representative of the HVO himself had the same impression. I want to ask him if he could give us some more clarification about what his impressions were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, are you able to directly answer the question for the Judge?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: If I'm to understand, it was the BiH representatives who were amazed at the accusation and the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant both the representative of the BH army and yourself, and I'm going to correct my own question, did you have the same impression? After the interpretation given by Mr. Cerkez, could you give us some more details about what impression you had?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: The impression I had was that it was impossible for the BiH to perpetrate such an act against themselves. With the extent of the damage, with the extent of the casualties, that it was impossible for the BiH to have done that to their own people and that it had to have been HVO troops who actually perpetrated Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you become aware of complaints on the part of BiH forces concerning the HVO's use of civilians as human shields on front lines between, particularly, the areas of Vitez and Stari Vitez, as well as the use of Muslim civilian prisoners to dig trenches on these front lines?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes. We encountered several incidents where accusations had been made that the HVO around the Stari Vitez area were using civilians and prisoners of war both to dig trenches and to provide human shields to protect their soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you do something about this enquiry, this concern?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes. We made several investigations and visits to those locations, and on one specific occasion made an appointment with Mario Cerkez to discuss the situation in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just for the benefit of those following the outline, there would be a jump in this response to number 47, but we can either go on or just go in order. Could you describe your encounter with Mr. Cerkez, if you had one, and what his explanation was? What was done on his part?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: The chairman of the ECMM, Henk Morsink, and I had a meeting with Mr. Cerkez in Vitez to really get permission to investigate, on a more thorough basis, the grounds of the accusations being laid against his troops. Again we met with a very flippant response, to the point that he said that Muslims were burning Croat houses in and around the Kruscica area and that we had to investigate that first before we could really investigate the use of prisoners and human shields.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you, nonetheless, respect the request of Mr. Cerkez and check this out, and did you do it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes, we checked thoroughly with one of his representatives on the ground and visited several locations to try and identify these burning houses, but found nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In what area were these houses allegedly burning?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: They were allegedly burning in the Kruscica area, between Vitez and Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the usher would distribute Z2612,3.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, if you would be kind enough to indicate the location of Kruscica on this map.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Kruscica is here [indicates], just a short distance south of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was a representative of Mr. Cerkez's present when the location, the alleged location, was given?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes. This was discussed with Mr. Cerkez, his representative, Henk Morsink, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was that individual also unable to locate any burning houses?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: We escorted him personally to several areas that were pointed out, and he could not identify any burning buildings in the whole of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What conclusion did you come to about the veracity of the complaint?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Our conclusion was that again it was a distraction to take our attention away from the accusations of using troops to dig trenches and using prisoners to act as shields in and around the Vitez area, so that we were detracted from investigating that fully by going on a bit of a wild-goose chase.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you find it to be false?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: We found the whole accusation of the burning houses completely false, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In order to save time, I was going to offer the same video clips that were shown during Mr. Morsink's testimony just to indicate that Mr. Buffini was, in fact, present, as well as to show one segment which has been provided to the Defence on the excerpts or actually on the entire tape of Mr. Buffini at the site of the examination of the dead bodies of two BiH soldiers. I think, if the Court has no objection, unless the Court wants to see it now, it will save considerable time. Again, the point was to confirm his presence there, and also, I think it will be available for you to view later, if you care to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Returning to the issue of trench digging, the use of Muslim detainees for trench digging, and mistreatment of Muslim prisoners, did the ICRC express a concern about this as well?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Yes. The ICRC came into several of our meetings. Ms. Claire Podbielski represented the ICRC and complained very bitterly towards the assembled group of HVO-BiH that this was unacceptable in the terms of the Geneva Convention and that it had to stop immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were these complaints of Ms. Podbielski's, as well as anything you had information on, raised with the HVO, with Mr. Nakic, with Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: Because most of the incidents, the accusations, were against the HVO, Ms. Podbielski directly made the accusations to Mr. Cerkez, Mr. Nakic, and other local commanders that were present at our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What were the responses?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: The response was that the HVO would not do such acts, they were against the Geneva Convention, and that they did not know of incidents where this was happening, so flat-out denial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was that outright denial by Cerkez, Nakic, or both?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: It was by both, and the other commanders as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you and Henk Morsink investigate the report of the bodies of two Muslim soldiers having been recovered? And if you could describe what you did about that report to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: We received a complaint from the local commander -- Bosnian Muslim commander in Kruscica that two bodies had been recovered after about 22 days in the open and had been brought back to a small village, where they asked us to inspect the bodies because they had signs of torture and mutilation. So we went to investigate at the village given to us but understood that the bodies had had to be buried that morning because of their state of decay. But a Muslim reporter had actually videoed the bodies before they were buried, which he then allowed us to see on his video camera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What were your observations when you viewed the videotape that was made?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL LESLIE BUFFINI
utterances.text: The videotape confirmed that the bodies were in a very bad state of decay, with maggots over most of the body, and flies, but it clearly shows that the neck had been severely cut, probably by a thin wire, strangulation, but very definite marks there. There were also very definite lacerations, deep lacerations, around both wrists on one body, as well as several fingers missing on one of the bodies which had been filmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, it's coming up to 1.00. Are you moving on to another topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, if it's convenient to stop and I will take ten minutes in the morning to finish, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Buffini, I'm afraid you'll have to come back tomorrow, half past 9.00, please, to finish your evidence. Could you remember, in this adjournment and any others there may be, not to speak to anybody about your evidence, and that includes the Prosecution, and of course not to allow anybody to speak to you about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Half past 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of November, 1999, at 9.30 a.m.
